title: Kernel
body:
The part of the [[Operating System]] that runs privileged. On the [[Motorola 68000]] that
means it runs in [[Supervisor State]], with the S bit of the [[Status Register]] set, and
can therefore do the things user code cannot: touch protected memory, program the
[[68901 MFP]] and other device registers, change the [[Interrupt Mask]], and switch the
processor between modes.

Everything else the OS ships (shell, compiler, editor, libraries) runs in user mode like any
other program. "Kernel" names the privileged core, not the whole system.

## The boundary

Two hardware facts create it, and this course gives you both:

1. **A privilege bit.** The processor knows which mode it is in and refuses privileged
   instructions in user mode, raising a privilege violation (8 bombs, see
   [[Assembly Errors]]) instead.
2. **A controlled doorway.** User code cannot simply `jsr` into the kernel, because that
   would jump to privileged code without changing privilege. It has to raise an exception,
   which is what a [[System Call]] is.

Interrupts cross the same boundary from the other direction: taking an interrupt always
enters supervisor state, which is why an [[ISRs|ISR]] is kernel code whether it looks like
it or not. See [[Interrupts]].

## What it is responsible for

Process scheduling, memory management, the file system, and device drivers. Each of those is
a unit of [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]; here they are just the reason the privileged half needs to
exist. The design question of how much to put inside it (monolithic kernel versus
microkernel) is [[Operating System Structure]]'s problem, not this course's.

The [[CPU]] itself knows none of this. It does not know which addresses are protected or
which code is the kernel; it only enforces the mode bit and reports faults. The policy is
entirely software.
